beats.text: In 1910, a 14-year-old girl in Michigan City lost both of her parents. And she inherited a freight car fortune.
beats.label: MICHIGAN CITY, INDIANA
beats.credit: History: Chicago Tribune, 1910; Barker Mansion marker

beats.text: Her name was Catherine Barker. Her father, John H. Barker, ran the Haskell and Barker Car Company, one of the biggest freight car builders in the country.
beats.label: HASKELL & BARKER
beats.credit: National Register of Historic Places; The Conservation Center

beats.text: He turned the family home on Washington Street into a 38-room mansion.
beats.label: WASHINGTON STREET
beats.credit: Barker Mansion marker; The Conservation Center

beats.text: Then, in 1910, Catherine's mother died. Before the year was out, her father died too.
beats.credit: Chicago Tribune, Dec. 4, 1910; Barker Mansion marker

beats.text: Newspapers put her inheritance in the millions. She grew up to start a foundation that still carries the family name.
beats.label: THE HEIRESS
beats.credit: Chicago Tribune, 1910; The New York Times, 1915; The Conservation Center

beats.text: In 1968, the mansion was given to the people of Michigan City. It's now a museum you can tour, May through December.
beats.label: TODAY
beats.credit: Barker Mansion and Barker Civic Center markers

beats.text: Comment your town, and it could be next.

end_card.pill: Barker Mansion, Michigan City: open May to December
